output.name: Hannel
output.myth: Hesk was quick. When Aun cut the string the sky ran up so fast the year's sailcloth nearly tore from the Reel, and she hung a weight on the Lamp Road: a grey stone with a hole through it, tied to goat-gut. Hannel does not sing or sleep. It keeps the warp straight so the year can be woven without a snag. A fist to the north-west hangs Mirrak, the Water Bag, which Aun, shouting at the wind, never thought to bring. A fist to the south-east Tekma sits on her wet ledge, oil in her gut, and needs no weight to hold her. Every winter Tavo comes down the cord and shakes it, laughing, to see if it will swing. Sil watches from the drowned lantern of her face; when the moon is thin she says it still hangs. Ennu says that is all a good weight ever does. My mother's mother said the day Hannel swings, every sail we own will split along its seams, and the Gulls will come down to pick up the pieces. So mind your knots, child, and count your stitches.
output.finding: From Mirrak, the Water Bag, Hannel lies one fist (about 10°) to the south-east on the same Lamp Road.
